entries.tile_summary: Quinoline yellow is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent yellow-green shade.
entries.expanded_summary: Quinoline yellow is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent yellow-green shade. It is a manufactured dye rather than a colour extracted from a food or plant.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for a stable yellow-green colour in foods and drinks.

entries.tile_summary: Indigotine, also called indigo carmine, is a blue synthetic food colour related in structure to indigo dye.
entries.expanded_summary: Indigotine, also called indigo carmine, is a blue synthetic food colour related in structure to indigo dye.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by chemical synthesis and purified as a water-soluble blue colour salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Produces deep blue shades and can be blended with yellow colours to make green.
entries.fact_2_copy: The food additive is manufactured; it is not the traditional plant-extracted indigo dye.

entries.tile_summary: Caramel I is a brown colouring made by controlled heat treatment of sugars or other food-grade carbohydrates.
entries.expanded_summary: Caramel I is a brown colouring made by controlled heat treatment of sugars or other food-grade carbohydrates. It is a colour ingredient, not simply the caramel made when sugar is browned in a kitchen.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by heated carbohydrates without ammonium or sulphite compounds, creating a complex mixture of brown colour compounds.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plain caramel.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to give foods and drinks brown to dark-brown colour.

entries.expanded_summary: beta-apo-8′-Carotenoic acid ester is a carotenoid-type yellow-orange colour structurally related to naturally occurring carotenoids, but food-grade material is manufactured as a defined colour ingredient.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled chemical synthesis and formulated to protect the colour from oxidation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for yellow to orange colouring.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its molecular family is the same broad pigment family that includes beta-carotene.

entries.tile_summary: Rhodoxanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with red colouring.
entries.expanded_summary: Rhodoxanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with red colouring. It belongs to the same broad natural pigment family as beta-carotene and lutein.
entries.source_preparation_copy: This carotenoid occurs in natural biological sources; commercial food-colour preparations may depend on the approved source and manufacturing specification.
entries.fact_1_copy: A xanthophyll carotenoid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for red colouring where permitted.

entries.expanded_summary: Metallic aluminium used for a silver-grey decorative effect where permitted.

entries.tile_summary: Potassium sorbate is the potassium salt of sorbic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium sorbate is the potassium salt of sorbic acid. It is used in food mainly for preservation rather than for flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising sorbic acid with potassium hydroxide or another potassium source, producing a water-soluble sorbate salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: One of the sorbate preservatives.
entries.fact_2_copy: Widely used to inhibit moulds and yeasts.
entries.evidence_copy: An Australian total-diet study measured sorbates in foods and combined the results with food-consumption data. Even the high-consumer estimates were no more than 40% of the group safety limit. The study used older consumption data, so it is not a current market census, but it provides direct Australian exposure evidence and did not identify a concern for ordinary dietary patterns.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: Australia and New Zealand food regulator: 21st Australian Total Diet Study (2005 report; current FSANZ archive)

entries.tile_summary: Propylparaben is the propyl ester of p-hydroxybenzoic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Propylparaben is the propyl ester of p-hydroxybenzoic acid. It is used in food mainly for preservation rather than for flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by esterifying p-hydroxybenzoic acid with propyl alcohol and purifying the product.
entries.fact_1_copy: A paraben preservative.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for antimicrobial preservation where permitted.

entries.expanded_summary: Potassium metabisulphite is the potassium counterpart of sodium metabisulphite and a solid source of sulphur dioxide-related preservative species.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting sulphur dioxide with a potassium alkali and crystallising the metabisulphite salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Part of the sulphite preservative family.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for preservation and antioxidant action, including in some beverage processes.

entries.tile_summary: Potassium nitrite is an inorganic nitrite salt.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium nitrite is an inorganic nitrite salt. In foods it is associated mainly with curing and preservation, particularly in meat processing.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced industrially as a purified inorganic nitrite salt from mineral or chemical starting materials.
entries.fact_1_copy: Nitrite and nitrate chemistry is used to control microbes and help develop characteristic cured-meat colour and flavour.
entries.fact_2_copy: This is a nitrite salt; nitrate can be converted to nitrite under some curing conditions.

entries.tile_summary: Calcium acetate is an acetate salt derived from acetic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium acetate is an acetate salt derived from acetic acid. It provides acetate chemistry without adding acetic acid in exactly the same form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising acetic acid with a calcium-containing base; diacetate forms also contain associated acetic acid.
entries.fact_1_copy: Chemically related to the acid found in vinegar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the salt and food, can help regulate acidity, preserve or influence flavour.

entries.tile_summary: Potassium propionate is the potassium salt of propionic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium propionate is the potassium salt of propionic acid. It is used mainly as a mould-inhibiting preservative.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising propionic acid with a potassium-containing base and purifying the resulting salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Commonly associated with preservation of bread and other bakery products.
entries.fact_2_copy: Releases propionate, the active acid-related preserving species, under food conditions.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium ascorbate is the calcium salt of ascorbic acid — vitamin C.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium ascorbate is the calcium salt of ascorbic acid — vitamin C. It provides ascorbate antioxidant chemistry in a salt form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising purified ascorbic acid with a calcium-containing base; the ascorbic acid itself is usually produced from glucose by industrial fermentation/chemical processing.
entries.fact_1_copy: It is chemically related to vitamin C and supplies ascorbate.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for antioxidant, colour-protection or processing effects.

entries.tile_summary: Gamma-tocopherol is one of the naturally occurring tocopherols in the vitamin E family.
entries.expanded_summary: Gamma-tocopherol is one of the naturally occurring tocopherols in the vitamin E family. It is fat-soluble and can help slow oxidation.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food-grade material is commonly isolated and purified from vegetable-oil fractions rich in tocopherols.
entries.fact_1_copy: Found naturally in vegetable oils and other plant foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as an antioxidant in fat-containing foods.

entries.expanded_summary: Sodium erythorbate is the sodium salt of erythorbic acid, a close chemical relative of vitamin C. It is used to provide antioxidant and colour-stabilising effects in a readily soluble form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising erythorbic acid with a sodium source and purifying the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Commonly used for antioxidant effects and to support cured-meat colour chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Related to vitamin C chemistry but not used as a significant vitamin source.

entries.expanded_summary: Potassium lactate is the potassium salt of lactic acid. It keeps the familiar lactic-acid chemistry but in a less acidic salt form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising lactic acid — commonly produced by fermentation of sugars — with a potassium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from lactic acid, the acid associated with many fermented foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the salt, can regulate acidity, retain moisture, firm texture or support preservation.

entries.tile_summary: Potassium citrate / potassium dihydrogen citrate is a potassium salt of citric acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium citrate / potassium dihydrogen citrate is a potassium salt of citric acid. It is used when food technologists want citrate chemistry with less direct acidity than citric acid itself.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising fermentation-produced citric acid with a potassium-containing base and crystallising the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from citric acid, the acid naturally associated with citrus fruit.
entries.fact_2_copy: Commonly used to regulate acidity, buffer pH or provide mineral/citrate functionality.

entries.tile_summary: Phosphoric acid is an inorganic acid based on phosphorus.
entries.expanded_summary: Phosphoric acid is an inorganic acid based on phosphorus. Unlike citric or lactic acid, it is not a fruit- or fermentation-derived organic acid.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Food-grade phosphoric acid is manufactured from phosphate mineral starting materials or highly purified phosphorus-derived intermediates.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to acidify foods and drinks and to control pH.
entries.fact_2_copy: It is the parent acid of the phosphate salts used elsewhere in food processing.
entries.evidence_copy: After consumption, the phosphate from 338 joins phosphorus from the rest of the diet. Europe's food-safety authority therefore assessed total exposure rather than treating one drink or additive code in isolation. The group safety value was considered protective for healthy people, but it expressly does not apply to those with moderate or severe loss of kidney function, who may clear phosphorus less effectively. The relevant exposure is total dietary phosphorus, not 338 alone.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of phosphoric acid and phosphates E338-341, E343, E450-452 (2019)

entries.tile_summary: Agar is a gel-forming carbohydrate mixture extracted from red seaweed.
entries.expanded_summary: Agar is a gel-forming carbohydrate mixture extracted from red seaweed. Its strong, heat-reversible gels are why agar is used both in foods and in laboratory culture media.

entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a gelling, thickening and stabilising agent.
entries.fact_3_copy: Agar gels set firmly and generally melt at a higher temperature than they set.

entries.tile_summary: Tragacanth gum is a complex gum exuded naturally from Astragalus shrubs.
entries.expanded_summary: Tragacanth gum is a complex gum exuded naturally from Astragalus shrubs. It is a plant-derived hydrocolloid used to manage texture and water in foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Collected or extracted from plant exudate from Astragalus species, then cleaned, milled and/or purified to food-grade specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: A high-molecular-weight carbohydrate rather than a simple sugar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for thickening, stabilising or controlling texture.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol that tastes sweet but behaves differently from ordinary sugar.
entries.expanded_summary: Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol that tastes sweet but behaves differently from ordinary sugar. It occurs naturally in some fruits, while commercial sorbitol is usually made from glucose.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Typically produced by hydrogenating glucose from starch-derived syrups; sorbitol syrup contains sorbitol plus related hydrogenated carbohydrates.
entries.fact_1_copy: Found naturally in fruits such as apples, pears and stone fruit.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a sweetener, humectant, bulking agent or texture modifier.
entries.evidence_copy: Sorbitol is only partly absorbed in the small intestine. Larger amounts can draw water into the bowel and be fermented, causing gas or loose stools; the amount that triggers symptoms varies between people and products. A United Nations food-additive expert committee did not consider a numerical toxicological limit necessary for its assessed uses. Australia and New Zealand require relevant foods to state that excess consumption may have a laxative effect. That statement describes a short-term, dose-related gut effect rather than cumulative toxicity.

entries.evidence_source_2_link_label: United Nations food-additive expert committee: Sorbitol INS 420 evaluation (1982)

entries.tile_summary: Polysorbate 60 is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived material, polyoxyethylene chains and stearic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Polysorbate 60 is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived material, polyoxyethylene chains and stearic acid. Its molecular design gives it both water-friendly and fat-friendly parts.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by esterifying sorbitol/sorbitan with fatty acids and adding polyoxyethylene chains through controlled chemical processing.
entries.fact_1_copy: Helps oils, fats and water stay mixed and can stabilise foams or dispersions.
entries.fact_2_copy: The fatty-acid feedstock may come from plant or animal fats, while the final emulsifier is chemically processed.

entries.tile_summary: Pyrophosphates are condensed phosphate salts in which phosphate units are linked together; this Schedule 8 number covers several sodium and/or potassium forms.
entries.expanded_summary: Pyrophosphates are condensed phosphate salts in which phosphate units are linked together; this Schedule 8 number covers several sodium and/or potassium forms. Compared with simple phosphates, their chain structure gives different water-binding, buffering and texture effects.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by heating and condensing purified phosphate salts under controlled conditions, then forming the required sodium or potassium salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Two phosphate units linked together.
entries.fact_2_copy: Can act in raising systems, moisture retention, emulsification, sequestration or texture control depending on the food.
entries.evidence_copy: Once eaten, 450 joins the same phosphorus pool as other phosphate additives and naturally occurring phosphorus. Europe's food-safety authority found some child exposure estimates above the group safety value, which does not apply to people with moderate or severe kidney impairment. A single ingredient list cannot show total phosphorus exposure, but repeated use of phosphate additives across staple foods can contribute to it.

entries.tile_summary: Methyl cellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose.
entries.expanded_summary: Methyl cellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose. Introducing methyl groups changes cellulose from an insoluble plant fibre into a material with useful thickening, film-forming or stabilising behaviour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with purified plant cellulose, which is reacted under controlled conditions to introduce methyl groups; the product is then washed and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant cellulose, commonly from wood pulp or cotton-derived material.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a thickener, stabiliser, film former or texture modifier depending on the derivative.

entries.consumer_display_name: Mono- and di-glycerides of fatty acids
entries.entry_title: Mono- and di-glycerides of fatty acids (471)
entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: E471 helps fat and water mix in foods. But its fatty acids may come from plants or animals — and the number alone won't tell you which.
entries.expanded_summary: Think of E471 as a mixing helper. It contains glycerol joined to one or two fatty acids, compared with three in typical dietary fats. Food manufacturers use it to help manage texture and mixing. Its fatty acids may come from vegetable oils or animal fats — the additive number cannot reveal which source was used in a particular product.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Usually made by reacting glycerol with fatty acids, or by rearranging edible fats and oils. The fatty acids can come from vegetable oils or animal fats — the additive number alone does not say which.
entries.fact_1_copy: Normal dietary fats are triglycerides; these are closely related partial glycerides.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as emulsifiers to help manage the boundary between fat and water.
entries.fact_3_copy: If plant or animal origin matters to you, look for product-specific sourcing information or trustworthy certification. The number 471 alone cannot confirm it.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority judged that digestive enzymes are very likely to split 471 into glycerol and fatty acids — the same broad components released when ordinary fat is digested. It found no evidence of gene damage, cancer or harm to reproduction at the assessed uses, and did not consider a numerical daily limit necessary. Estimated intake from 471 contributed only about 0.8–3.5% of recommended daily fat intake at the mean.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids E471 (2017)

entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced industrially by electrolysis of purified brine.
entries.fact_1_copy: A strongly or moderately basic sodium-containing compound used for processing rather than flavour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its technical name can sound severe because concentrated material is reactive; food use is controlled and application-specific.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium ferrocyanide is an inorganic complex salt used mainly as an anticaking agent.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium ferrocyanide is an inorganic complex salt used mainly as an anticaking agent. Despite the word 'cyanide' in the chemical name, the cyanide groups are tightly bound within a stable iron-cyanide complex rather than present as free cyanide.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by forming and crystallising a controlled ferrocyanide complex with potassium ions.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used at low levels to keep salt and other powders free-flowing.
entries.fact_2_copy: The compound is chemically distinct from free hydrogen cyanide or simple cyanide salts.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium aluminosilicate is a porous inorganic aluminosilicate.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium aluminosilicate is a porous inorganic aluminosilicate.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by precipitation from sodium, aluminium and silicate solutions.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used mainly as an anticaking agent in dry powders.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Stearic acid and related food fatty acids are long-chain fatty-acid molecules — the same basic components that make up ordinary dietary fats and oils.
entries.expanded_summary: Stearic acid and related food fatty acids are long-chain fatty-acid molecules — the same basic components that make up ordinary dietary fats and oils.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained by splitting and purifying plant or animal fats/oils; some fatty acids can also be produced from other industrial starting materials.
entries.fact_1_copy: Triglyceride fats are built from glycerol plus fatty acids such as stearic, palmitic and oleic acid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as processing aids, anticaking agents, glazing aids or building blocks for other emulsifiers.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number alone does not reveal plant versus animal origin.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Magnesium gluconate is the magnesium salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose.
entries.expanded_summary: Magnesium gluconate is the magnesium salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose. The gluconate part is highly water-compatible and can bind minerals.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from fermentation/oxidation-derived gluconic acid followed by neutralisation with a magnesium-containing source.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glucose-derived gluconic acid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the mineral, used for mineral delivery, acidity control, sequestration, colour stabilisation or processing.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Monoammonium L-glutamate is the ammonium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste.
entries.expanded_summary: Monoammonium L-glutamate is the ammonium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste. It belongs to the same glutamate flavour-enhancer family as MSG.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Glutamic acid is commonly produced by microbial fermentation of sugars or starch hydrolysates, then neutralised with a ammonium source to make the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glutamate occurs naturally in foods including tomatoes, mushrooms, seaweed and aged cheeses.
entries.fact_2_copy: The glutamate ion provides savoury umami taste.
entries.fact_3_copy: Added glutamate and naturally occurring glutamate are the same glutamate ion once dissolved in food.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Ethyl maltol is a synthetic relative of maltol with a much stronger sweet, caramel-like aroma.
entries.expanded_summary: Ethyl maltol is a synthetic relative of maltol with a much stronger sweet, caramel-like aroma. A small structural change from maltol makes its flavour-enhancing effect more intense.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled chemical synthesis and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Adds or strengthens sweet, caramel, jammy and confectionery-like notes.
entries.fact_2_copy: It is an ethyl-substituted version of maltol and is generally more potent.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used as a flavour enhancer, not as a high-intensity sweetener.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with animal or insect material. The target substance is separated from that material and then cleaned, refined or converted into a stable food-grade form.
entries.tile_summary: Shellac is a natural resin secreted by lac insects on host trees.
entries.expanded_summary: Shellac is a natural resin secreted by lac insects on host trees. It is refined into a hard, glossy coating used on foods and many non-food products.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Resinous lac material produced by insects is collected from branches, cleaned, melted or solvent-refined and formed into food-grade shellac.
entries.fact_1_copy: Insect-derived resin rather than a plant wax.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a glazing and protective coating.
entries.fact_3_copy: Its insect origin can matter for vegan or personal ingredient choices.

entries.source_profile_definition: A purified gas used in or around food. It may dissolve into the product, displace oxygen in a package, create bubbles or foam, or act as a propellant.
entries.tile_summary: Butane is a small hydrocarbon gas.
entries.expanded_summary: Butane is a small hydrocarbon gas.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Separated and purified from natural-gas and petroleum-refining streams.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a propellant in specified food applications; it evaporates readily after dispensing.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Isomalt is a sugar alcohol mixture made from sucrose.
entries.expanded_summary: Isomalt is a sugar alcohol mixture made from sucrose. It looks and behaves more like a bulk sugar ingredient than an ultra-intense sweetener.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Sucrose is first rearranged enzymatically and then hydrogenated, producing a mixture of hydrogenated sugar alcohols that is purified and crystallised.
entries.fact_1_copy: Ordinary sucrose.
entries.fact_2_copy: Less sweet than sucrose, so it contributes bulk as well as sweetness.
entries.fact_3_copy: Common in sugar-free confectionery because it can provide structure, glassy texture and lower sweetness.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Neotame is a very high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame but modified so it is far sweeter and behaves differently in the body.
entries.expanded_summary: Neotame is a very high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame but modified so it is far sweeter and behaves differently in the body.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by chemically modifying aspartame-related amino-acid components and purifying the resulting compound.
entries.fact_1_copy: Several thousand times sweeter than sucrose.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used at extremely low levels for intense sweetness.
entries.fact_3_copy: Structurally related to aspartame but it is a distinct sweetener.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Advantame is an ultra-high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame.
entries.expanded_summary: Advantame is an ultra-high-intensity synthetic sweetener structurally related to aspartame. A chemical modification dramatically increases its sweetness potency.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting aspartame-related material with a vanillin-derived intermediate, then purifying the resulting compound.
entries.fact_1_copy: Tens of thousands of times sweeter than sucrose under some test conditions.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used at extremely low levels for intense sweetness.
entries.fact_3_copy: It is related to aspartame structurally but is a distinct molecule with different properties.

entries.source_profile_definition: A protein that performs a specific biological job. Food enzymes may be extracted from plants or animals, or produced by microorganisms grown by fermentation. They speed up reactions such as breaking starch, protein or fat into smaller components.
entries.tile_summary: Lysozyme is an antimicrobial enzyme that attacks a structural component of many bacterial cell walls.
entries.expanded_summary: Lysozyme is an antimicrobial enzyme that attacks a structural component of many bacterial cell walls. Commercial food lysozyme is traditionally isolated from hen egg white.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commonly extracted and purified from egg white, then standardised as an enzyme preparation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Lysozyme is part of natural antimicrobial defence and occurs in egg white, tears and other biological fluids.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to control certain bacteria in applications such as cheese and wine.
entries.fact_3_copy: Traditional food-grade lysozyme is egg-derived, which matters for allergen and ingredient-source considerations.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Bleached starch is starch treated with permitted oxidising/bleaching agents mainly to improve colour and remove impurities.
entries.expanded_summary: Bleached starch is starch treated with permitted oxidising/bleaching agents mainly to improve colour and remove impurities. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes controlled bleaching/oxidation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Acetylated distarch phosphate is phosphate-cross-linked starch with added acetyl groups.
entries.expanded_summary: Acetylated distarch phosphate is phosphate-cross-linked starch with added acetyl groups. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes cross-linking plus acetylation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Acetylated oxidised starch is oxidised starch that also carries acetyl groups.
entries.expanded_summary: Acetylated oxidised starch is oxidised starch that also carries acetyl groups. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes oxidation plus acetylation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Quillaia extract type 1 is a less-purified saponin-rich extract made from the bark or wood of the soapbark tree, Quillaja saponaria.
entries.expanded_summary: Quillaia extract type 1 is a less-purified saponin-rich extract made from the bark or wood of the soapbark tree, Quillaja saponaria. Its key components are saponins — plant molecules that can stabilise foam and emulsions.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by water extraction of soapbark tree material, followed by filtration and concentration; type 2 undergoes more extensive purification than type 1.
entries.fact_1_copy: Quillaja saponaria, a South American tree also called soapbark.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a foaming agent and emulsifier, especially in beverages.
entries.fact_3_copy: The types differ mainly in purification and composition, not in the basic plant source.
